learning_objective: 🎯 Discover the essential economic activities that involve extracting and utilizing resources directly from nature, forming the base of human survival!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: These are economic activities directly dependent on the environment. They involve the utilization of earth's resources like land, water, vegetation, building materials, and minerals.
The oldest economic activities. People rely on their immediate environment for survival, gathering wild plants and hunting animals. It requires very little capital and technology.
Rearing animals. It can be 'Nomadic Herding' (moving with herds to find water/pastures) or 'Commercial Livestock Rearing' (highly organized, capital-intensive farming on permanent ranches).

Ranges from 'Subsistence Agriculture' (growing just enough to feed the farmer's family) to 'Plantation Agriculture' (growing single cash crops like tea/coffee for profit) and 'Extensive Commercial Grain Farming'.
Extracting valuable minerals from the earth. Can be done via surface/open-cast mining (cheaper and easier) or underground/shaft mining (deeper, riskier, and more expensive).

fun_activity.title: ☕ The Journey of a Coffee Bean
fun_activity.instructions: Think about your morning coffee or tea. Map out its primary activity roots—how it was grown on a plantation, hand-picked, and processed before becoming a secondary product. You are consuming primary agriculture!

exam_tips: 📌 Understand the difference between Nomadic Herding (traditional, subsistence) and Commercial Livestock Rearing (modern, profit-driven).
📌 Memorize the characteristics of Plantation Agriculture: large estates, high capital, scientific methods, and single-crop specialization.
📌 Know the two main types of mining: open-cast (surface) and shaft (underground) mining.
quick_recap: ⭐ Primary activities are directly tied to extracting resources from nature.
⭐ Subsistence agriculture is divided into primitive (shifting cultivation) and intensive (feeding high density populations).
⭐ Mixed farming involves both cultivating crops and raising livestock simultaneously to balance income.
